Governance models must include mechanisms for democratic oversight and community engagement, ensuring that those most affected by AI interventions have a voice in their design and implementation.

In practice, this requires institutional channels, including citizen assemblies, standing patient and public involvement panels, and statutory consultation obligations on regulators, that give affected communities a formal role in shaping which AI tools are approved, how they are deployed, and under what conditions they are withdrawn.

unlisted_practices: Laws and regulations should incentivize the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of health data following the FAIR guiding principles.
Regulators should require minimum representativeness standards for AI training data and evaluation as a condition of market access and reimbursement.
Payers and regulators should offer enhanced incentives to AI developers who demonstrate exceptional commitment to equity.
Payers and governments should reform payment models from fee-for-service toward bundled, value-based payments that reward equitable, high-quality AI use, with clear standards defining value.

Regulators and HTA bodies should embed repeated-sampling designs, demographic subgroup analyses, a priori acceptability thresholds, and equity-specific endpoints as structural requirements rather than optional additions.
Regulators should develop adaptive regulatory mechanisms that require revalidation of AI tools as they change.
Policymakers should integrate climate and environmental impact into AI evaluation frameworks.
Policymakers should establish international coordination on minimum AI standards with LMIC participation in governance design.
Data governance frameworks should enable meaningful consent, community control, and equitable benefit-sharing, including data-sharing provisions with LMICs.
Health systems should systematically integrate AI competencies into medical curricula and equitably resource AI training across the workforce.
Regulators should address whether AI preserves patients' capacity for autonomous choice, not only whether it improves their information.
Policymakers should align AI regulation with health system governance through interdisciplinary collaboration among data scientists, ethicists, clinicians, regulators, and citizens.
Regulators and funders should define suitable end-points for AI-focused health research and HTA.
Regulators should require robust auditability protocols and real-world performance monitoring with agreed endpoints for AI.
